transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-11
Start: 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood Solutions Eng); Sofia Ruiz (Aurigent Platform Eng), Tom Hayes (Aurigent ML Infra), Priya Malhotra (Aurigent SRE), Nikhil Rao (Aurigent CTO)
Shared artifacts: link: https://redwood.internal/slides/compute-slice-kv-warmup (deck), link: drive/aurigent/benchmarks (logs)

Summary (auto-gen, rough): Focused on a couple of levers to raise sustained throughput without blowing latency SLOs: 1) compute-slicing (time-sliced GPU lanes / tile scheduling) to reduce head-of-line blocking, 2) adaptive token caps per-customer that scale with observed KV hit-rate, 3) proactive KV warmup / prefetch policies for on-prem VPC where cold caches are common. Discussed tradeoffs for quantized models and continuous batching implications.

Topics covered:
- Intro & goals: Aurigent needs 2-3x steady throughput upgrade for inference pipelines with minimal tail-latency regression, must operate within VPC and meet SOC2 logging needs.
- Compute slicing: concept, how it prevents single long seqs from stalling others.
- Adaptive token caps: soft limits, dynamic scaling with cache hit-rate and compute availability.
- KV warmup strategies: synthetic prefixing, partial prefetch windows, and background pre-population.
- Scheduler knobs: max_num_seqs, slot size, burst token ceilings, eviction aggressiveness.
- Quantization interactions: int8 vs int4 behavior when packing sequences; perf regressions at small batch sizes.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, let's kick off. we've got about 50 minutes, goal is to land on a concrete bench plan and a config to try.
[00:16] Nikhil Rao: yep thanks, we want to get more throughput on our in-house chat assistant, right now steady-state is fine but during peaks we see big tail spikes and cold-cache slowdowns.
[00:23] Ravi Patel: quick clarifying q — when you say "cold-cache slowdowns" is that 95th vs p50 or full blow 99.9th?
[00:29] Tom Hayes: mostly 95/99, p50 is okay. but we also have long sequences that sometimes block others; the current scheduler tends to pack them and then under continuous batch it holds an entire slot for a long time.
[00:42] Lena Ortiz: ok, so we should talk about two axes: per-request sequencing (max_num_seqs) and a runtime slicing approach so a single long sequence doesn't hog the GPU.
[00:53] Sofia Ruiz: we run in a VPC on prem hardware, can't rely on cross-tenant cache hits. KV cache tends to be cold after redeploys, that's happening a lot.
[01:05] Ravi Patel: right and that means simple prefix caching won't help unless we prewarm or do predictive fetches. the other lever is adaptive token caps — say you give a soft ceiling of tokens/sec per tenant that scales up as KV hit-rate rises.
[01:22] Tom Hayes: can you explain compute slicing in plain terms?
[01:25] Maya Chen: yeah, think of slicing as dividing GPU time into multiple interleaved lanes — we schedule partial work for long sequences so they yield periodically; you still make progress on the long seq but shorter requests can run between slices. reduces head-of-line blocking.
[01:40] Ravi Patel: practical knobs: tile_size (or slice quantum), slice_preempt_threshold, and a short max_inflight_per_seq. setting tile_size too small increases kernel launch overheads; too big and you don't avoid blocking.
[01:52] Priya Malhotra: do we need kernel-level changes or is this at the runtime scheduler layer?
[01:56] Ravi Patel: mostly runtime scheduler; the runtime already supports partial kv evict/restore so we can preempt without losing KV pointers. there are micro-optimizations but you won't need a custom kernel for the basic approach.
[02:12] Nikhil Rao: and how does this interact with continuous batching? i.e., when idle we batch constantly, doesn't that reintroduce head-of-line?
[02:20] Lena Ortiz: good question — continuous batching groups by arrival window and sequence length heuristics; compute slicing complements that by limiting per-sequence inflight work inside a batch. so you get the per-token efficiency of batching while preserving fairness.
[02:35] Maya Chen: important practical trade: if you have heavy quantization (int4), kernel latency per token drops but variance increases — micro-slicing can amplify jitter if your tile quantum is mis-configured.
[02:47] Tom Hayes: is there a rule of thumb for tile_size vs quantization?
[02:51] Ravi Patel: empirically we start with tile_size ~ 8-16 tokens for int8, and 4-8 for int4; again depends on model and kernel amortization. smaller tiles for int4 tends to keep latency tail lower but increases overhead.
[03:05] Sofia Ruiz: okay, how about adaptive token caps — you mentioned scaling with KV hit-rate, can you walk through that flow?
[03:11] Ravi Patel: sure. baseline: you set a soft token cap per-tenant, e.g., 500 tokens/sec. runtime monitors KV hit-rate and effective token throughput; if hit-rate > 80% for a sliding window, the cap can increase (linear or exponential backoff) up to a configured max. conversely, if hit-rate drops (cold cache), cap is reduced and requests get queued or routed to a cheaper fallback.
[03:34] Maya Chen: design considerations: 1) cap changes must be slow enough to avoid oscillation, 2) we need safety fallback paths — either reroute to a smaller model variant or return degraded tokens with a confidence/quality flag, 3) observability hooks to show per-tenant hit-rate and cap history.
[03:50] Priya Malhotra: our compliance team will want logs correlating cap changes to request IDs — do you ship that?
[03:55] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Console can emit token cap change events and include request sampling. we can also stream audit logs into your SIEM.
[04:03] Nikhil Rao: the KV warmup piece — you said synthetic prefixing and partial prefetch windows earlier. explain the difference and safety concerns.
[04:10] Ravi Patel: synthetic prefixing is creating warmup requests that load likely KV keys (e.g., common system prompts or templated user prefixes) into cache prior to traffic. prefetch windows are runtime heuristics that, when we observe a new user activity, we prefetch the next N tokens' KV entries in background. both risk additional load — need to budget for warmup bandwidth and make sure it doesn't evict hot keys.
[04:30] Tom Hayes: does Redwood provide warmup tooling?
[04:33] Maya Chen: yes, we have a warmup job script (we shared a deck) — it can replay representative prompt sets at controlled QPS, and there's a "prefetch budget" you can tune.
[04:42] Lena Ortiz: also consider partial prewarm: warm the top-k KV keys instead of full sequences, that reduces memory churn.
[04:49] Sofia Ruiz: on prem our cluster has constrained network to storage, so we want a warmup pattern that minimizes I/O. is there a way to prepopulate just the in-GPU KV slots?
[04:58] Ravi Patel: yes, the runtime supports an in-memory KV pre-population API — essentially you push serialized KV blobs into runtime memory during maintenance windows. we recommend incremental warmups during deployments.
[05:10] Maya Chen: maybe let's sketch an experiment: two runs, identical arrival patterns. Run A: no prewarm. Run B: prewarm top-100 tokens per active user with controlled QPS. Compare 95/99 latency and sustained throughput.
[05:22] Tom Hayes: sounds good. about scheduler knobs, you mentioned max_num_seqs — what's your recommended starting value?
[05:27] Ravi Patel: depends on GPU and model size, but for mid-size LMs we'd start with max_num_seqs = 64 for gpus with 80GB-class memory, or 24-32 for smaller devices; the point is to limit total concurrent sequences so KV memory and batch packing are predictable. it's also tied to slot_size and token ceiling.
[05:44] Nikhil Rao: we run multiple tenants, can adaptive token caps be per-tenant and still fair?
[05:50] Lena Ortiz: yes, the runtime supports per-tenant soft quotas and global fairness windows. we recommend a per-tenant long-window token budget and a short-window burst allowance that's gated by KV hit-rate.
[06:00] Sofia Ruiz: curious about fallback model variants — you said route when KV hit-rate low. what about quality regressions?
[06:06] Ravi Patel: fallback should be an explicit policy: route low-hit requests to a cached smaller quantized variant or local on-device model and tag outputs as "degraded". we also support automatic A/B quality checks so you can measure drift.
[06:18] Tom Hayes: we have a strict SLO on hallucination — reduced models might be risky. can we instead queue excess tokens and return partial responses?
[06:25] Maya Chen: yes, graceful degrade options include: queue with expected delay, return partial streaming outputs, or route to a smaller model with a confidence flag. it's a tradeoff between latency and accuracy.
[06:34] Priya Malhotra: operationally, what are common failure modes when enabling compute slicing?
[06:38] Ravi Patel: two common ones: 1) over-aggressive preemption causing thrash (too small tile_size), 2) interaction with quantization kernels that have non-linear latency behavior causing tail spikes. both are fixable by tuning slice quantum and adding jitter to schedule boundaries.
[06:53] Nikhil Rao: what's the trick for the "adaptive" part so it doesn't oscillate?
[06:56] Lena Ortiz: use exponential smoothing with a high time constant for the metric (e.g., 5-10 minute EWMA) and require consecutive windows above threshold before increasing cap; on decrease you can be a bit faster but still use hysteresis. also, cap changes are stepped.
[07:11] Tom Hayes: are there built-in dashboard widgets for these metrics?
[07:14] Maya Chen: yes, we've got per-tenant KV hit-rate, cap history, queue length, and a simulated "what-if" slider to preview throughput if we increase caps.
[07:24] Sofia Ruiz: can you share example scheduler config?
[07:27] Maya Chen: will do — we'll attach recommended profiles: conservative, balanced, aggressive. for your case I'd suggest balanced first.
[07:34] Ravi Patel: in the repo we gave an example YAML: max_num_seqs, tile_size, slice_preempt_threshold_ms, slot_token_ceiling, warmup_prefetch_budget. we'll send it after call.
[07:47] Priya Malhotra: about metrics collection, how intrusive is the sampling?
[07:51] Lena Ortiz: sampling is lightweight; by default we sample 1% of requests for full traces and log aggregated counters for every tenant at 10s granularity. can increase if you need more fidelity.
[08:01] Nikhil Rao: any gotchas with VPC/on-prem? network egress for warmup, and KMS integration for encryption?
[08:07] Maya Chen: for on-prem/VPC we support local prewarm so it doesn't hit external storage. KMS/HSM integration is supported for keys; we can do local HSM or bring-your-own KMS. we'll include docs.
[08:17] Tom Hayes: let's talk numbers — if we enable compute slicing + warmup, what kind of throughput lift have you seen?
[08:22] Ravi Patel: in customer cases where cold stalls were dominant, we've seen 1.5-3x effective sustained throughput improvements while keeping 95th latency within 10-20% of baseline. results vary widely.
[08:33] Sofia Ruiz: what's a practical pilot you recommend?
[08:36] Maya Chen: Run the two-run benchmark I mentioned, plus a 24-hour pilot with adaptive token caps enabled in monitor-only mode for one tenant. collect metrics for hit-rate, cap changes, queue times, and user-perceived latency.
[08:48] Tom Hayes: ok we'll do that.
[08:50] Maya Chen: for the bench harness we'll give you a script that can replay your production arrival distribution — it supports toggles for synthetic warmup and different tile_size settings.
[09:00] Priya Malhotra: what's the expected extra CPU/memory overhead of warmup?
[09:04] Ravi Patel: warmup uses bandwidth and some CPU; if you use the in-Runtime prepopulation API it's mostly memory and minimal CPU because it writes KV blobs directly. background prefetch uses I/O and network. budget the warmup QPS so it doesn't overthrow the serving plane.
[09:18] Nikhil Rao: a question about eviction policies — do you have a TTL per KV entry?
[09:22] Lena Ortiz: we have LRU-ish heuristics plus explicit sticky lists for pinned keys. you can configure TTLs, hot-list sizes, and a low-watermark eviction threshold to avoid churn.
[09:33] Tom Hayes: what about multi-tenant fragmentation of KV memory — is there isolation?
[09:38] Maya Chen: in Dedicated or Private you can pin per-tenant KV quotas and soft isolation; we can reserve KV memory by tenant or shard. that helps avoid eviction storms from noisy neighbors.
[09:49] Sofia Ruiz: can we test per-tenant reservations in pilot?
[09:52] Maya Chen: yes, we'll include a config to reserve 25% KV mem for your high-priority tenant.
[09:58] Ravi Patel: ok, some concrete tuning recommendations for the bench: start with max_num_seqs = 48, tile_size = 12 tokens, slice_preempt_threshold_ms = 20ms, slot_token_ceiling = 512 tokens, warmup_prefetch_budget = 200pps; run warm vs cold and capture 95/99.
[10:17] Tom Hayes: those numbers look reasonable. please put them in the follow-up email as YAML.
[10:21] Maya Chen: will do.
[10:23] Priya Malhotra: any other design concerns with quantization?
[10:26] Ravi Patel: normative: int8 is easier, lower variance; int4 gives better throughput but you want slightly larger tile_size to amortize jitter. also ensure your quantization pipeline preserves KV serialization format.
[10:39] Nikhil Rao: what about long-running streams where users keep context and KV grows — how to bound memory?
[10:45] Lena Ortiz: strategies: aggressive windowing (evict older context beyond N turns), hierarchical caching (local ephemeral + remote persistent), or offload older KV shards to cold storage with fast-refill if accessed. each has cost/latency tradeoffs.
[10:58] Tom Hayes: let's discuss observability anchor points we should collect for the pilot so we can evaluate success.
[11:02] Maya Chen: collect: per-tenant KV hit-rate (1s/10s windows), queue length, slot occupancy, per-request tokens, cap change events, latency p50/95/99, and model quality signals (loss or sampling-based checks).
[11:17] Ravi Patel: add spike detection alerts for sudden KV hit-rate drops or a cascade of cap reductions; these often indicate infra flaps.
[11:26] Priya Malhotra: any auto-rollbacks?
[11:29] Maya Chen: yes, we have auto-fallback where if p99 latency crosses threshold for >2mins after a config change, the system can rollback or route to previously stable model variant.
[11:40] Nikhil Rao: good. one more thing — security and audit: will the warmup payloads be logged? we don't want sensitive prompts to be stored in plaintext.
[11:48] Lena Ortiz: warmup should use sanitized prompts; runtime can redact or hash sensitive tokens before logging. we can also keep warmup logs in encrypted storage only.
[11:58] Tom Hayes: perfect.
[12:00] Maya Chen: ok team, to recap: Redwood will send config YAML + bench harness script; Aurigent will run warm vs cold runs and a 24h pilot with adaptive token caps monitor-only. we'll reconvene after logs are in.
[12:13] Sofia Ruiz: sounds good, thanks.
[12:15] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. ending soon.
